newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: INTERVIEW-Sumitomo Chemical hikes Singapore output.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Sumitomo Chemical hikes Singapore output.

text.p: Sumitomo Chemical is aggressively expanding its production base in Singapore to capture the growing southeast Asian petrochemical market, company president Akio Kosai said on Tuesday.
"Our Singapore petrochemical capacity is now the same size as in Japan," Kosai told Reuters in an interview.

In Japan, Sumitomo has an ethylene plant in Chiba prefecture with an annual capacity of 380,000 tonnes. It also has a 22.5-percent stake in Keiyo Ethylene, which operates Japan's largest plant with an annual capacity of 600,000 tonnes.
Sumitomo has already invested more than US$500 million to double its ethylene, polyethylene and polypropylene production capacity in Singapore.
Sumitomo and three other Japanese companies on Tuesday began construction of six plants costing $300 million to produce acrylic acid and its derivatives.

The company leads a consortium of Japanese companies that owns 50 percent of the city-state's sole ethylene producer -- the Petrochemical Corporation of Singapore (PCS). The remaining 50 percent is owned by Royal Dutch Shell.
PCS over the weekend started its new 515,000-tonne-per-year ethylene plant, taking its total capacity to 965,000 tonnes.
The new plant is the heart of a Singapore $3.4-billion (US$2.36 billion) expansion that includes The Polyolefin Co (TPC), in which Sumitomo owns 55 percent.
TPC, a key derivative plant of the new complex, produces polyethylene and polypropylene, which are used to make plastic products for both consumer and industrial markets.
Kosai said TPC over the weekend also started polyethylene production with polypropylene output slated for later this week.
The new units raised TPC's polyethylene annual output to 350,000 tonnes and polypropylene to 313,000 tonnes.
"In this area (Southeast Asia), demand during 1997 and 1998 is very good," Akio said. Analysts said Southeast Asian polymer demand was forecast to grow by 10 percent a year to 2000.
Kosai said when Sumitomo made its initial investments in Singapore in the early 1980s, there were few captive endusers.
But rising manufacturing costs in Japan and a strong yen forced many electronics and industrial companies to shift their production base to Singapore and Southeast Asia, he said.
"After the stronger yen, many plants transferred to this area and so we built our plants here," Kosai said.
Sumitomo also holds a 20-percent share in Phillips Petroleum Singapore Chemicals' 380,000-tonne-per-year polyethylene plant.
Kosai said the start-up of the new plants in Singapore should contribute to improved company earnings in the next financial year.
Kosai said the company was recently streamlined to cut costs in the face of difficult operating conditions in Japan and he hoped to reap the benefits soon.
He said the Japanese petrochemical sector was slowly recovering, and companies were thinking of raising product prices. "The domestic demand is growing strongly but price is not so good."
